concept.name: Duration
concept.definition: A measure of a bond's price sensitivity to changes in interest rates, expressed in years; formally, the Macaulay duration is the present-value-weighted average time to receipt of the bond's cash flows, and it serves as the basis for the price-sensitivity (modified duration) measure.
concept.intuition: Duration compresses maturity, coupon, and yield into one number that approximates how many percent a bond's price moves when rates move one percent — the bond's interest-rate speedometer.
concept.mechanics: Macaulay duration = sum over t of [t x PV(CF_t)] / price. Longer maturities and lower coupons raise duration; a zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity, while coupon bonds always have duration below maturity. Approximate percentage price change = -duration (modified) x yield change.
concept.formula: Macaulay duration D = [ sum_t t x CF_t / (1+y)^t ] / P, where CF_t = cash flow at time t, y = yield per period, P = bond price.
concept.failure_modes: Duration is a linear (first-order) approximation that degrades for large rate moves (where convexity matters) and assumes parallel yield-curve shifts; for callable or mortgage-backed bonds, changing cash flows make static duration unreliable (effective duration is used instead).
concept.misconceptions: Duration is not the same as maturity: except for zero-coupon bonds it is shorter than maturity, and it is a risk measure, not a waiting period; nor is it constant — it drifts with time, yield, and coupon changes.
concept.example: A 10-year bond with a 5% coupon might have a duration near 8-9 years, so a 1% rise in rates implies roughly an 8-9% price decline, versus under 1% for a 6-month bond.
